warmup.q: A loop runs Point p = new Point(i, i + 1); sum += p.x() + p.y(); a million times, and p is never stored anywhere. Once the method has run many times and the JVM's optimizing compiler (C2) has compiled it, how many bytes does one call allocate?
options: It depends on the heap size
warmup.why: C2's escape analysis sees that p never leaves the method, so it keeps x and y in registers and never creates the object. In the lesson's JDK 25 run, the first three rounds allocated megabytes while the code ran in the interpreter and C1, and every later round allocated 0. With -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis, every round allocated 32,000,000 bytes. The heap size plays no part.

opening:
Back in the warehouse, new boxes arrive all day. Picture every worker walking to the floor manager's desk with each new box to ask where it should go. The queue at that desk would soon be longer than the work. So each worker reserves a stretch of empty shelf, and puts every new box in the next free spot of their own stretch, without asking anyone.

That's how the JVM creates objects. In the last lesson, every box cost its label plus its fields: 40 bytes for a Thumbnail. Putting one on the shelf costs a few machine instructions. And sometimes, when a box never leaves a worker's desk, the JVM doesn't make it at all.

Two traps sit on either side of that. One says allocation is free, so never think about it. The other says allocation is slow, so reuse objects. Both are wrong, and in useful ways.

In this lesson, we'll watch threads claim their stretches of shelf, count the bytes a piece of code allocates, catch the JVM's compiler skipping a box, and find where a program's bytes really come from. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with workers who each reserve a stretch of shelf and fill it without asking anyone. The JVM does the same with TLABs, so a new is a pointer bump, and C2 skips the box entirely when it never leaves the desk. What costs you is the rate, and boxing is where most of it hides.

Now search your own code for String.format, Map<Integer, ...> or List<Long> inside a loop that runs for every request or every item. Each one is a box per pass.

Next, we'll ask which boxes the cleaning crew may throw away. Java lets you hold an object loosely, so what do soft, weak and phantom references promise?

sections.h: A private stretch of shelf: allocation is a pointer bump in a TLAB
sections.html:
New objects go into eden, the part of the heap set aside for new arrivals. (Lesson 4 explains why the heap has a separate area for them.) Every thread shares eden. If each new took its memory straight from eden, every thread would have to update one shared "next free byte" pointer. They'd take turns, like workers queueing at the floor manager's desk.

So each thread claims a chunk of eden for itself, its TLAB (thread-local allocation buffer), and allocates inside it with no locking at all. That's the reserved stretch of shelf. In the JDK 25 demo below, each chunk was about 500 KB, room for twelve thousand small arrays.

Allocating inside a TLAB means moving a "top" pointer forward, which is called bump-pointer allocation. This is HotSpot's fast path, from the JDK 25 source:

HeapWord* obj = top();
if (pointer_delta(end(), obj) >= size) {   // does the object fit?
  set_top(obj + size);                     // bump the pointer
  return obj;
}
return nullptr;                            // no: take the slow path

It's a compare, an add and a store. Then the JVM writes the object's header and zeroes its fields. Once a method is compiled by the JIT (the part of the JVM that turns busy bytecode into machine code), these few instructions sit right inside your code, so a new doesn't even make a call.

The slow path runs when the object doesn't fit. Usually the TLAB is simply full, and the thread claims a fresh one from eden with one atomic update, a single step that no other thread can interrupt. That's the only moment two threads' allocations can meet. Objects too big for a TLAB go straight into eden. G1, the JVM's default garbage collector, splits the heap into equal regions of 1 to 32 MB. An object bigger than half a region is humongous: a 3 MB photo in one byte[], on a heap with 2 MB regions, skips TLABs and eden entirely. Lesson 4 shows why that costs more.

Here the warehouse picture breaks, and the break teaches something. In a warehouse, carrying a box to its shelf is the hard part. In the JVM, the bump costs a few instructions, and the bill comes later. Every TLAB a thread fills brings eden closer to full, and a full eden is what calls the cleaning crew: a young collection, the GC run that empties eden.

So what you pay for is the allocation rate, the bytes allocated per second. A service that allocates 1 GB a second fills a 500 MB eden twice a second, and with G1 each of those is a pause, a moment when the program's threads stop while the collector works. The objects that are already dead cost almost nothing even then, because a young collection copies only the objects still alive. Kotlin compiles to the same new bytecode, so all of this is identical in both languages.

The rate, then, is worth measuring. How many bytes does one piece of code allocate? You don't have to guess.

try.title: Count TLAB refills
steps: Read TlabDemo. It allocates 5,000,000 arrays of 40 bytes, 200 MB in all, in a child JVM that logs a TLAB summary at every GC. Predict: how often will the main thread go back to eden for a fresh TLAB?
Run it with the command below.
Find the GC(1) TLAB totals line. Divide the megabytes that pause found by the number of refills.

code.title: TlabDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.memory.l02; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.util.List; /** * Allocates 5,000,000 small arrays in a child JVM that logs a TLAB summary at every GC. * Each "refills" count is how often a thread went back to eden for a fresh buffer. */ public class TlabDemo { static volatile Object sink; public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length == 0) { for (String line : Jvm.lines(List.of("-Xmx256m", "-Xlog:gc,gc+tlab=debug"), TlabDemo.class.getName(), "allocate")) { System.out.println(line.replaceAll("\\s+", " ")); } return; } for (int i = 0; i < 5_000_000; i++) sink = new byte[24]; // 16-byte header + 24 bytes = 40 bytes each System.out.println("allocated 5,000,000 arrays of 40 bytes: 200,000,000 bytes"); } }

alt.title: TlabDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.memory.l02 import workbench.memory.Jvm @Volatile private var tlabSink: Any? = null /** * Allocates 5,000,000 small arrays in a child JVM that logs a TLAB summary at every GC. * Each "refills" count is how often a thread went back to eden for a fresh buffer. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isEmpty()) { Jvm.lines(listOf("-Xmx256m", "-Xlog:gc,gc+tlab=debug"), "workbench.memory.l02.TlabDemoKt", "allocate") .forEach { println(it.replace(Regex("\\s+"), " ")) } return } repeat(5_000_000) { tlabSink = ByteArray(24) } // 16-byte header + 24 bytes = 40 bytes each println("allocated 5,000,000 arrays of 40 bytes: 200,000,000 bytes") }

try.expect: On JDK 25: GC(1) TLAB totals: thrds: 1 refills: 196 ... slow allocs: 0 ... waste: 0.1%, then Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 99M->1M. One thread allocated about 98 MB in 196 refills, so each TLAB held about 500 KB, roughly 12,500 arrays per trip to the shared eden. slow allocs: 0 means no array had to skip its TLAB. JDK 21 uses smaller TLABs (about 305 refills for 61 MB), and the counts change from run to run.

sections.h: Counting bytes with the thread's allocation counter
sections.html:
HotSpot counts every byte each thread allocates. A ThreadMXBean is the JDK's management interface for facts about threads, and com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean, an extension of the standard one, hands you the counter with getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() (since JDK 14). Read it, run the code, read it again:

Java
var threads = (com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean) ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean();
long before = threads.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes();
byte[] photo = new byte[1 << 20];
long bytes = threads.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - before;   // 1,048,592
Kotlin
val threads = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() as com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean
val before = threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes
val photo = ByteArray(1 shl 20)
val bytes = threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes - before          // 1,048,592

The Javadoc calls the number "an approximation". For code that runs once, it's exact to the byte in practice: 1 MiB of data plus a 16-byte array header gave 1,048,592. That makes it the best way to test your model from the last lesson. A thousand Long boxes for values above the cache allocate 24,000 bytes, exactly 1,000 times 24.

The counter has two traps, and the demo below walks into both.

The first call to anything pays for one-time setup. The first Long.valueOf builds the JDK's cache of the 256 boxes from -128 to 127, and that cost 7,456 bytes on JDK 25. The first string concatenation sets itself up too: a thousand "img-" + i cost 100,480 bytes the first time and 48,000 the second, 48 bytes per name. Measure twice and trust the second number.

The second trap is a virtual thread, the lightweight kind of thread that the JDK runs on top of a few platform threads. There the counter returns -1, its polite way of saying "not here". Measure on a platform thread.

In a test, the pattern has three steps. Call the code once on tiny input, so its classes are loaded. Measure one call on real input. Then compare the bytes with what the result itself needs, plus a margin. A method that returns a long[500] needs 4,016 bytes. If it allocates 1.5 MB, something inside it is boxing. That comparison is deterministic, and it's exactly what the lab's tests do.

The counter answers questions like "which step of this request allocates?" For the allocation rate of a whole running program, use JFR (Java Flight Recorder, the JDK's built-in recorder) or the GC log. The performance track covers JFR, and lesson 6 of this track reads GC logs.

Sometimes, though, the counter reports 0 for code that plainly says new.

try.title: Predict four allocation counts
steps: Read AllocationCounterDemo (or the Kotlin twin). Write down your prediction for each line, for the first run and for the second.
Run it with the command below.
Explain each difference between the first column and the second.

code.title: AllocationCounterDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.memory.l02; import com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; /** Counts the bytes a few small pieces of code allocate, twice each, using the JVM's per-thread counter. */ public class AllocationCounterDemo { static final ThreadMXBean THREADS = (ThreadMXBean) ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean(); static volatile Object sink; // results escape here, so nothing is optimized away static long bytes(Runnable work) { long before = THREADS.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes(); work.run(); return THREADS.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - before; } static void show(String what, Runnable work) { long first = bytes(work); // the first run also pays for one-time setup long second = bytes(work); System.out.printf("%-34s %,10d %,11d%n", what, first, second); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { System.out.printf("%-34s %10s %11s%n", "bytes allocated by", "first run", "second run"); show("new byte[1 MiB]", () -> sink = new byte[1 << 20]); show("1,000 x Long.valueOf(i % 128)", () -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) sink = Long.valueOf(i % 128); }); show("1,000 x Long.valueOf(1_000 + i)", () -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) sink = Long.valueOf(1_000 + i); }); show("1,000 x \"img-\" + i", () -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) sink = "img-" + i; }); Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> System.out.println("on a virtual thread the counter says " + THREADS.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes())).join(); } }

alt.title: AllocationCounterDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.memory.l02 import com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory private val THREADS = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() as ThreadMXBean @Volatile private var sink: Any? = null // results escape here, so nothing is optimized away private fun bytes(work: () -> Unit): Long { val before = THREADS.currentThreadAllocatedBytes work() return THREADS.currentThreadAllocatedBytes - before } private fun show(what: String, work: () -> Unit) { val first = bytes(work) // the first run also pays for one-time setup val second = bytes(work) println("%-34s %,10d %,11d".format(what, first, second)) } /** Counts the bytes a few small pieces of code allocate, twice each, using the JVM's per-thread counter. */ fun main() { println("%-34s %10s %11s".format("bytes allocated by", "first run", "second run")) show("ByteArray(1 MiB)") { sink = ByteArray(1 shl 20) } show("1,000 x boxing (i % 128).toLong()") { for (i in 0 until 1_000) sink = (i % 128).toLong() } show("1,000 x boxing (1_000 + i).toLong()") { for (i in 0 until 1_000) sink = (1_000 + i).toLong() } show("1,000 x \"img-\$i\"") { for (i in 0 until 1_000) sink = "img-$i" } Thread.ofVirtual().start { println("on a virtual thread the counter says ${THREADS.currentThreadAllocatedBytes}") }.join() }

try.expect: On JDK 25, the 1 MiB array costs 1,048,592 bytes both times (the Kotlin twin's first run adds 40 bytes of one-time setup). Long.valueOf(i % 128) costs 7,456 bytes the first time, to build the box cache, and 0 after, because every value comes from the cache. Long.valueOf(1_000 + i) costs 24,000 both times. The string concatenation costs about 100,000 bytes the first time and 48,000 after: 48 bytes per name. On the virtual thread the counter says -1.

sections.h: The box that never leaves the desk: escape analysis
sections.html:
C2 is the JIT compiler that optimizes a program's hottest methods, and it pays close attention. First it does inlining: it copies the small methods a method calls into the method's own body. Then it runs escape analysis, which checks whether an object can be seen anywhere outside the method it's compiling. If it can't, C2 can skip the object and keep its fields in registers, the processor's own small storage slots. That step is called scalar replacement. In the warehouse, it's a worker noticing that a box never leaves the desk, and writing its contents on the notepad instead.

Here's a loop that makes a million short-lived points:

Java
record Point(long x, long y) {}

static long sumPoints(int n) {
    long s = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        Point p = new Point(i, i + 1);   // p never leaves the method
        s += p.x() + p.y();
    }
    return s;
}
Kotlin
data class Point(val x: Long, val y: Long)

fun sumPoints(n: Int): Long {
    var s = 0L
    for (i in 0 until n) {
        val p = Point(i.toLong(), i + 1L)   // p never leaves the function
        s += p.x + p.y
    }
    return s
}

A Point is a 12-byte header plus two longs, 28 bytes, padded to 32. So a call with n = 1,000,000 should allocate 32,000,000 bytes. Call it ten times and count each call on JDK 25:

round 0:    3,282,776 bytes
round 1:    1,572,832 bytes
round 2:      262,112 bytes
round 3:            0 bytes
...
round 9:            0 bytes

Same code, same new, zero bytes. With -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis, which switches the analysis off, every round allocated 32,000,000 bytes: a million 32-byte points.

Now look at the first rounds. The interpreter (which runs bytecode one instruction at a time) and C1 (the quick JIT compiler that runs first) create every object. The allocation only disappears once C2 has compiled the method, and when that happens depends on timing: one run of the Kotlin twin on JDK 21 reached 0 only at round 5. Here the warehouse picture breaks again. A person would notice the first time that a box never leaves the desk. C2 notices only after it has watched a method run thousands of times, and only inside the code it inlined.

Escape analysis is a bonus, not a promise. Never assert "allocates nothing" in a unit test. It can pass on your laptop and fail on a busier machine. The lab asserts only the allocations the code really needs.

An object escapes when you store it in a field, an array or a collection, return it, or pass it to a method C2 didn't inline. C2 also won't scalar-replace an array with more than 64 elements (the EliminateAllocationArraySizeLimit flag). So escape analysis helps tight loops. It can't help a design that keeps every size in a HashMap<Integer, Long>, because those boxes live on inside the map. And that's where most of a program's bytes come from.

try.title: Watch an allocation disappear, then bring it back
steps: Run EscapeDemo. It runs the measurement in two child JVMs: one with default flags, one with -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis.

Now make p escape. In the Java version add static Point last; to the class and last = p; inside the loop. In Kotlin add a top-level var last: KPoint? = null and last = p. Predict the new numbers, then run it again.
Remove the change when you're done.

code.title: EscapeDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.memory.l02; import com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.util.List; /** * Sums a million short-lived Points per round and counts the bytes each round allocates. * The demo runs the experiment twice, in child JVMs: with escape analysis, and without it. */ public class EscapeDemo { record Point(long x, long y) {} // 12-byte header + 16 bytes of fields: 32 bytes static long sumPoints(int n) { long s = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { Point p = new Point(i, i + 1); // p never leaves this method s += p.x() + p.y(); } return s; } public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length == 0) { System.out.println("== default flags: escape analysis on"); Jvm.run(List.of(), EscapeDemo.class.getName(), "measure"); System.out.println("== -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis"); Jvm.run(List.of("-XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis"), EscapeDemo.class.getName(), "measure"); return; } ThreadMXBean threads = (ThreadMXBean) ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean(); long checksum = 0; for (int round = 0; round < 10; round++) { long before = threads.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes(); checksum += sumPoints(1_000_000); long bytes = threads.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - before; System.out.printf("round %d: %,12d bytes%n", round, bytes); } System.out.println("checksum " + checksum); } }

alt.title: EscapeDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.memory.l02 import com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean import workbench.memory.Jvm import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory data class KPoint(val x: Long, val y: Long) // 12-byte header + 16 bytes of fields: 32 bytes fun sumPoints(n: Int): Long { var s = 0L for (i in 0 until n) { val p = KPoint(i.toLong(), i + 1L) // p never leaves this function s += p.x + p.y } return s } /** * Sums a million short-lived points per round and counts the bytes each round allocates. * The demo runs the experiment twice, in child JVMs: with escape analysis, and without it. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isEmpty()) { println("== default flags: escape analysis on") Jvm.run(listOf(), "workbench.memory.l02.EscapeDemoKt", "measure") println("== -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis") Jvm.run(listOf("-XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis"), "workbench.memory.l02.EscapeDemoKt", "measure") return } val threads = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() as ThreadMXBean var checksum = 0L for (round in 0 until 10) { val before = threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes checksum += sumPoints(1_000_000) val bytes = threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes - before println("round %d: %,12d bytes".format(round, bytes)) } println("checksum $checksum") }

try.expect: With default flags, the first few rounds allocate megabytes, then the count drops to 0 and stays there (from round 3 in the JDK 25 run behind this lesson). With -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis, every round allocates 32,000,000 bytes. After you add last = p, the default run also allocates 32,000,000 bytes in every round, because the point now escapes into a static field and C2 has to create it.

sections.h: Where the bytes really come from: boxing, strings and copies
sections.html:
Most of the allocation in a program doesn't come from the new statements you wrote. It hides in boxing (wrapping a primitive such as a long in an object such as java.lang.Long), in collection helpers and in strings. The lab's upload report is a typical case. It adds up the bytes each user uploaded today:

Java
Map<Integer, Long> totals = new HashMap<>();
for (int i = 0; i < userIds.length; i++) {
    totals.merge(userIds[i], sizes[i], Long::sum);   // boxes the key, the size and the sum
}
Kotlin
val totals = HashMap<Int, Long>()
for (i in userIds.indices) {
    totals.merge(userIds[i], sizes[i]) { a, b -> a + b }   // the same three boxes
}

For 20,000 uploads from 500 users, this allocates 1,539,040 bytes, about 77 bytes per upload. User ids above 127 become new Integer boxes, and every size and every running sum becomes a new 24-byte Long. The caller only needs one total per user: a long[500] of 4,016 bytes. Index the array by user id and you get the same answer with no garbage at all.

These are the usual suspects:

  • Boxed collections: List<Long>, Map<String, Integer>, and in Kotlin anything typed Long? or used as a type argument.
  • Helpers that copy: toList(), map {}, windowed, zip, and streams of boxed values.
  • Strings: each "img-" + i costs 48 bytes (a String and its array). String.format, the most expensive way to glue three values together, cost about 700 bytes per call in the worked example below.
  • Lambdas that capture local variables, which create a new object each time the expression runs.

Don't chase every allocation, though. A request that allocates 50 KB is fine. Fix the loops over large batches, and the code behind a young GC that runs several times a second. Measure, change one thing, and measure again.

A check before the lab. In Kotlin, sizes.map { it * 2 }.sum(), or in Java, sizes.stream().map(s -> s * 2).toList(), on a List<Long> of 10,000 sizes above 1,000 bytes. Count the objects each one creates and estimate the bytes. (About 10,000 new 24-byte Long boxes and a 40 KB array for the new list, so roughly 280 KB. The same loop over a LongArray creates nothing.)

The lab hands you the upload report's two methods. Both give the right answer, and both are wasteful. Your job is to make them allocate only their result.

aside.title: Should I reuse objects instead of creating new ones?
aside.html: For short-lived objects, no. A temporary object that dies in eden costs the collector almost nothing, because a young collection copies only survivors. A pooled object survives, so the collector copies it out of eden and later into the old generation, the heap's long-term storage, and every young object you store into it must be tracked by the write barrier from lesson 4. Pools also need locking and reset code, and a missed reset leaks one request's data into the next. Keep pools for things that are truly expensive to create: connections, threads and large buffers outside the heap.

compare.title: A file-size type with and without an object

java.title: FileSize.java
java.html: // Java: a record is always an object (escape analysis may remove short-lived ones) record FileSize(long bytes) { FileSize plus(FileSize other) { return new FileSize(bytes + other.bytes); } // a new 24-byte object } FileSize total = new FileSize(0); for (long s : sizes) total = total.plus(new FileSize(s));

kotlin.title: FileSize.kt
kotlin.html: // Kotlin: a value class is a plain long at runtime, unless it has to be boxed @JvmInline value class FileSize(val bytes: Long) { operator fun plus(other: FileSize) = FileSize(bytes + other.bytes) // compiles to long + long } var total = FileSize(0) for (s in sizes) total += FileSize(s) // no objects

compare.note: The Kotlin value class compiles to a raw long in fields, parameters and return types, so the loop allocates nothing, even in the interpreter. The Java record is a real object every time. C2 may scalar-replace the short-lived ones in a hot loop, but you can't count on it. The Kotlin version boxes as soon as the value is used as a type argument, a nullable type or Any: a List<FileSize> or a FileSize? holds boxed objects again, just as List<Long> does.

worked.title: Take the allocation out of a cache lookup

steps.say: The thumbnail service keeps finished thumbnails in a map, so a second request for the same photo at the same size is served from memory. The first version builds each lookup key with String.format. Measured with the allocation counter over 10,000 lookups in Java on JDK 25, it allocated about 712 bytes per lookup at first, and still 632 to 656 once the code was hot.
steps.code: // Naive: a varargs array, a Formatter, its buffers and the string, per lookup byte[] find(String name, int width, int height) { return cache.get(String.format("%s@%dx%d", name, width, height)); }

alt.html: // Naive: a varargs array, a Formatter, its buffers and the string, per lookup fun find(name: String, width: Int, height: Int): ByteArray? = cache["%s@%dx%d".format(name, width, height)]

steps.say: 1. Build the same string with plain concatenation. The Java version allocated 64 bytes per lookup: a 24-byte String and a 40-byte array for the 19 letters of photo-0.jpg@160x120. Once the code was hot, 40 bytes.
steps.code: byte[] find(String name, int width, int height) { return cache.get(name + "@" + width + "x" + height); }

alt.html: fun find(name: String, width: Int, height: Int): ByteArray? = cache["$name@${width}x$height"]

steps.say: 1. Drop the string. A record key holds the three values as they are, and its equals and hashCode come for free. It's a 12-byte header, one reference and two ints: 24 bytes per lookup. And once C2 had compiled the lookup, the counter read 0, because the key never escapes find, so C2 scalar-replaced it. With -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis it stayed at 24.
steps.code: record ThumbKey(String name, int width, int height) {} final Map<ThumbKey, byte[]> cache = new HashMap<>(); byte[] find(String name, int width, int height) { return cache.get(new ThumbKey(name, width, height)); }

alt.html: data class ThumbKey(val name: String, val width: Int, val height: Int) val cache = HashMap<ThumbKey, ByteArray>() fun find(name: String, width: Int, height: Int): ByteArray? = cache[ThumbKey(name, width, height)]

steps.say: 1. Check that nothing changed but the bytes. In the run behind these numbers, all three versions found all 100 cached thumbnails, and the formatted key equals the concatenated one. Then put the saving in context: at, say, 2,000 lookups a second, the first version makes 1.4 MB of garbage a second and the record at most 48 KB. That's worth a change on a path that runs for every request, and not worth one on a path that runs once a minute.

lab.title: Make the upload report allocate only its result
steps: Run the tests. Five of seven fail. The two that pass check the answers: the report's code is correct, only wasteful. Read the failure messages: bytesByUser allocates 1,539,040 bytes where its result is 4,016.
Write AllocationMeter.bytesAllocatedBy: read the counter, run the block, read it again. Throw IllegalStateException if the counter is -1, which is what a virtual thread gets.
Rewrite bytesByUser with one LongArray(userCount) indexed by user id.
Rewrite rollingSums with a running sum: add up the first window sizes, then for each step add the size that enters the window and subtract the one that leaves.
Run the tests until all seven pass.
hints: for (i in userIds.indices) compiles to a plain index loop over the array. It allocates no iterator and no range object.
The tests call each method once on tiny input before they measure. That loads every class the method uses, so one-time setup doesn't count against you.
The allocation tests allow 512 bytes above the result array. Any boxing at all blows through that: 20,000 boxes are 480,000 bytes.

drill.title: Write the allocation meter from memory
drill.prompt: Close the page. Write a function that returns the number of bytes a block of code allocates on the current thread. Make it refuse to run where the counter doesn't work. Which threads are those?

answer.html: static final com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean THREADS = (com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean) ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean(); static long bytesAllocatedBy(Runnable block) { long before = THREADS.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes(); if (before < 0) throw new IllegalStateException("no counter here: use a platform thread"); // -1 on a virtual thread block.run(); return THREADS.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - before; }

alt.html: private val THREADS = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() as com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean fun bytesAllocatedBy(block: () -> Unit): Long { val before = THREADS.currentThreadAllocatedBytes check(before >= 0) { "no counter here: use a platform thread" } // -1 on a virtual thread block() return THREADS.currentThreadAllocatedBytes - before }

recap: Each thread allocates inside its own TLAB, a chunk of eden, by bumping a pointer. Only a refill touches shared memory, and G1's humongous objects skip TLABs entirely.
new is cheap. The allocation rate is what costs you, because it decides how often eden fills and a young collection runs.
com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() counts a thread's bytes exactly. Measure twice to skip one-time setup, and never on a virtual thread, where it returns -1.
C2's escape analysis can remove an object that never leaves a compiled method. It only happens after C2 compiles the code, so show it in demos and never assert it in tests.
Most allocation hides in boxing, copying helpers and strings. Use primitive arrays and plain keys in hot loops, and measure before and after each change.
The limit of today's tools: the counter says how many bytes a piece of code allocates, not how long they live. Whether they cost the collector 1 ms or 100 ms depends on what survives.

explain.prompt: A colleague says: "Allocation is free on the JVM, so I never think about it." Explain in your own words what is true in that, and what is missing.
explain.answer: The allocation itself is nearly free. Each thread owns a TLAB in eden and allocates by bumping a pointer, with no locking, and dead young objects cost the collector almost nothing because it only copies survivors. What's missing is the rate. Every byte allocated brings the next young collection closer, so a hot path that boxes every value or formats a string per lookup makes the collector run more often. Escape analysis can remove some short-lived objects, but only after C2 compiles the code and only if they never escape. So don't fear new, but measure the bytes in big loops and per-request paths, and remove boxing there.

deeper.html:
The TLAB trace has more in it than the summary the demo prints. With -Xlog:gc+tlab=trace, each refill prints a line like this one from JDK 25:

TLAB: fill thread: 0x00007f96ec01a030 [id: 20675] desired_size: 512KB slow allocs: 0  refill waste: 8192B alloc: 0.92801    20906KB refills: 44 waste  0.1% gc: 0B slow: 26144B

desired_size is the TLAB size the JVM aims for with this thread. It adapts to how fast the thread allocates and how many threads share eden. refill waste is the most free space the JVM is willing to throw away to start a new TLAB. When an object doesn't fit and less than that is left, the thread abandons the rest of its TLAB and claims a new one. When more is left, the thread keeps its TLAB, puts that one object directly in eden, and counts a slow allocation. The abandoned tail of a TLAB is filled with a dummy object so the heap stays easy to walk, and the waste percentage counts those tails.

Escape analysis helps with locks too. If an object never escapes, no other thread can ever lock it, so C2 can drop the synchronized blocks on it (the EliminateLocks flag). A local StringBuffer, whose methods are all synchronized, is the classic example.

Finally, the counter you used is per thread. getThreadAllocatedBytes(long[] ids) reads it for other threads too. For a whole program, JFR records allocation samples with stack traces, so it can show which code allocates the most. The per-second rate from JFR or the GC log tells you whether allocation is a problem at all; the per-block counter then tells you where the bytes come from.
